01 / ABOUT

My Biography

My name is Mohammed Junaid Mohamad Ismail. On this website, I introduce myself publicly as Mohammed Junaid. I am a Rohingya student born in Myanmar, and my interests include education, technology, programming, and the future of my community.

My Story, Learning Journey, and Ambitions

I believe that every person has a story still being written. Mine is a journey of learning, discovering new interests, building confidence, and thinking about how I can use knowledge to make a positive contribution. I am a student, and I know that education is not only about completing lessons or passing examinations. It is also about becoming curious, learning how to ask better questions, solving problems patiently, and understanding the world beyond what we already know.

I am currently studying toward my GED and am also a student in R.E.I and REC. These parts of my education are important steps in my development. I want to keep improving my English, strengthen my general knowledge, and build a solid foundation for future study. I understand that progress takes time. Some things are easy to learn, while others require practice, patience, and the willingness to try again. I want to keep moving forward one step at a time.

Technology is one of the areas that excites me most. I am interested in programming and coding because they allow people to turn ideas into practical things. A program begins with a problem or an idea, then grows through planning, writing instructions, testing, finding mistakes, and improving the result. I find this way of thinking valuable because it teaches patience and problem-solving. I hope to develop my abilities further and learn how to build useful digital projects as my experience grows.

Taking part in the R.ED Code coding competition was an important milestone in my learning journey. I achieved first place and received a prize and a certificate. I am proud of this achievement because it represents an opportunity I took part in and a result I worked toward. I see it not as the end of my learning, but as encouragement to continue practising, explore new challenges, and become more capable. I hope to add more projects, training, and accomplishments to this website over time as I gain new experience.

My identity as a Rohingya person is also an important part of my story. The Rohingya have deep roots in Myanmar, particularly in Rakhine State, and our community has faced severe discrimination, displacement, and barriers to basic rights. The history of my people includes painful events, but our identity should never be reduced to suffering alone. Rohingya people have culture, language, family connections, knowledge, creativity, faith, hopes, and dreams for the next generation. I want visitors to understand both the challenges our community faces and the humanity, dignity, and potential of Rohingya people.

I believe that learning and sharing reliable information can help people understand one another. Human rights should apply to everyone, regardless of background or identity. Every child deserves access to education; every family deserves safety; and every community deserves to live with dignity. I hope for a future in which Rohingya children can learn in safe classrooms, families can live without fear, and people can preserve their identity while enjoying equal rights and opportunities. I want this website to encourage respectful understanding rather than hatred, and to support justice, peace, and accountability through peaceful and lawful means.

Beyond the details listed here, I am still discovering my strengths and the kind of work I want to do in the future. I do not believe a person needs to have every answer at the beginning. What matters is continuing to learn, staying open to new ideas, treating people fairly, and making an honest effort. I want to become more skilled in technology, gain experience through real projects, and use what I learn in ways that are useful to other people.

The values I want to carry forward are education, curiosity, compassion, fairness, respect, perseverance, and hope. I want to listen to people whose experiences differ from mine, learn from mistakes, and keep working toward my goals. My achievements so far are part of a beginning, and I hope the pages of this website will grow as I continue my studies and projects.

This website brings together my education, interests, achievements, and commitment to sharing awareness about Rohingya history and human dignity. It is a public introduction to the person I am becoming: a student who wants to learn, a beginner in technology who wants to keep building, and a Rohingya young person who hopes for a future shaped by knowledge, equal rights, peace, and opportunity. My journey is ongoing, and I look forward to adding new chapters as I learn and grow.

02 / HERITAGE

My People, My Roots

The Rohingya are a Muslim ethnic minority with deep historical roots in Myanmar, particularly in Rakhine State. Our identity, language, culture, family ties, and memories are important parts of who we are. I include this section to help visitors learn about Rohingya people with respect and humanity.

Our Struggles

For decades, many Rohingya have faced discrimination, restrictions on movement, barriers to education and healthcare, displacement, and difficulties obtaining citizenship or legal identity. These conditions affect families’ safety, opportunities, and hopes for the future. Every person deserves dignity, protection, and equal rights.

Human RightsEducationDisplacement

The 2017 Atrocities and Genocide

In 2017, a major military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State drove more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh. United Nations investigators reported genocidal acts, and the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the attacks as genocidal. The Rohingya continue to seek safety, recognition, justice, and the ability to live with rights and dignity. This section aims to inform, remember those affected, and support accountability through peaceful and lawful means.

RememberJusticePeace

Our Culture and Humanity

Rohingya people are more than the hardships we have faced. We have families, traditions, languages, skills, dreams, and young people who want to learn and build a better future. Our stories deserve to be heard with care, and our community deserves to be treated with humanity.

My Hope for the Future

I hope for a future where Rohingya children can study safely, families can live without fear, people can preserve their identity, and everyone can enjoy equal rights. I believe learning, respectful dialogue, and sharing reliable information can help people understand one another.

Why this matters: Sharing reliable information is one way to honour people affected, encourage understanding, and support human dignity.

HERITAGE / CONTINUED

The Rohingya Genocide & the Crisis Today

Remembering what happened, understanding what continues, and standing for dignity, safety, and justice.

What Happened in 2017

In August 2017, a military crackdown in Myanmar's Rakhine State forced more than 700,000 Rohingya people to flee to Bangladesh. Families lost their homes and communities were uprooted. United Nations investigators documented grave atrocities and found evidence of genocidal intent. The events of 2017 remain central to the Rohingya community's call for truth, accountability, and justice.

The Crisis Has Not Ended

Rohingya people still face insecurity, discrimination, displacement, and severe restrictions on basic rights. Renewed conflict in Rakhine State has placed civilians in danger, and access to food, healthcare, education, and humanitarian support remains difficult for many. The United Nations reported in 2026 that conditions were not yet suitable for refugees to return safely and voluntarily.

Life Without Equal Rights

Statelessness and barriers to citizenship have left many Rohingya families without the protections and opportunities others take for granted. Displacement can interrupt schooling and separate people from their homes and livelihoods. Every child deserves education, every family deserves safety, and every person deserves recognition and equal treatment.

Justice, Peace & Our Future

As a Rohingya student, I want people to learn about my community through reliable information and compassion. Remembering past atrocities should go hand in hand with protecting people today. I hope for accountability, freedom from discrimination, safe and voluntary return when conditions allow, and a future in which Rohingya young people can study, work, and thrive with dignity.
